body_markdown:
# **The Gender Wage Gap Is Finally Closing Again as More Women Are Back at Work, but Not Everyone Is Benefiting**


### **Key findings:**


-


The gender wage gap narrowed in 2025. Women working full-time year-round now earn $0.84 for every dollar their male peers make.


-


More women than men work in nonfarm roles, as the rise in healthcare jobs over the past year has bolstered women’s employment opportunities.


-


Not all women are seeing the same improvements: Black women have seen their wage gap continue to widen, and despite having the highest growth in labor force participation, Hispanic women still see the largest wage gap.


### **A step in the right direction: the gender wage gap narrows**


**New**[Census Bureau income data](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2026/demo/income-poverty/p60-289.html) **shows the gender wage gap narrowed in 2025. Women working full-time year-round now earn $0.84 for every dollar their male peers make** , up from $0.81 in the year before. Why does that matter? For two consecutive years (2023 and 2024), the gap[widened](https://nwlc.org/press-release/for-the-first-time-ever-census-bureau-data-shows-gender-wage-gap-widening-for-a-second-year-in-a-row/) ; the first time in history there were back-to-back years of decline. And the 2025 improvement is the first statistically significant jump[since 2016](https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/2026/demo/p60-289.pdf) , so it’s genuine progress. It’s encouraging. But at the current pace, full pay parity, especially for women of color, could still be[decades away](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/amid-rising-costs-the-gender-wage-gap-deepens-affordability-challenges-for-women/#:~:text=On%20the%20current%20trajectory%20for%20full%2Dtime%2C%20year%2Dround%20workers%2C%20it%20would%20take%20women%20another%2045%20years%20to%20close%20the%20wage%20gap%3A%20If%20the%20gender%20wage%20gap%20continues%20on%20the%20same%20path%20it%20took%20from%202000%20to%202025%2C%20it%20would%20take%20until%202071%20for%20it%20to%20close%20for%20women%20working%20full%20time%2C%20year%2Dround.*) .


### **Better pay parity isn’t showing up in every woman’s paycheck**


Here’s the problem: while the overall gender wage gap improved by 3 cents between 2024 and 2025, the story looks very different when you break it down by race. Black women and Hispanic women aren’t seeing the same gains.


-


**Black women** : earn $0.64 per dollar (down from $0.69 in 2022)


-


**Hispanic women** : earn $0.60 per dollar


-


**Overall women** : earn $0.84 per dollar


Why did Black women’s gap get worse? Labor force participation for Black women dropped from 63.9% (2023 peak) to 61.9% now. That’s a big dip. Federal job cuts hit Black women especially hard; they make up a[disproportionately large share](https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/03/11/black-women-impacted-by-doge-cuts-are-rebuilding-their-careers.html) of government workers, so when those jobs disappeared, it affected them more than other groups. This could also have played a role in further worsening the racial gender wage gap, as many Black women had their careers disrupted.


Broader industry trends also help explain other changes in women’s employment and pay. As of this spring, more women work in nonfarm roles in the US than men. Healthcare is a major reason women’s employment has risen, as women account for nearly[80% of healthcare employees](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/healthcare/about/index.html#:~:text=Women%20represent%20nearly%2080%25%20of%20the%20healthcare%20work%20force.) and demand for those jobs keeps growing. Softening in historically male-dominated industries, like finance and information, has further cemented this shift.


Demand for healthcare workers is expected to remain strong for the foreseeable future, given the demographic need for healthcare services from an aging population. But that’s not the only driver pushing more women to the workforce. Women earn[most college degrees](https://hechingerreport.org/women-rule-in-college-and-graduate-and-professional-schools/#:~:text=Women%20now%20earn%2060%20percent%20of%20master%E2%80%99s%20and%C2%A0%20doctoral%20degrees%2C%20according%20to%20the%20U.S.%20Department%20of%20Education.) at all levels in the US, drawing more young women into the workforce and boosting women’s participation rates. The gap between women’s and men’s prime-aged employment rates has narrowed over the past several decades, as more women find opportunities in the labor force, and more men step away.


More opportunities in women-dominated fields and higher education rates are certainly foundational to the changes in women’s employment. But demographic shifts also play a role.


### **Hispanic women are driving the change**


Here’s how big of a shift this is when looking at the fastest-growing labor force demographic, Hispanic workers:


-


Hispanic workers now make up more than 1 in 5 U.S. workers


-


They accounted for 61% of labor force growth over the past decade


-


They’re expected to account for[all labor force growth](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/the-state-of-the-hispanic-workforce) over the next decade


Hispanic women are a particularly strong demographic shaping overall labor market dynamics, with the largest gain in labor force participation of any group over the last two decades. Aside from women of other races, all racial/ethnic groups for both sexes saw declining participation rates.


And Hispanic women will likely be the main source of growth over the next decade. According to[BLS employment projections](https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/civilian-labor-force-summary.htm) , Hispanic women not only saw the fastest growth in employment between 2015 and 2025, but they are also expected to be the only group to see a growing labor force over the next 10 years.


But despite being a growing engine of the overall US labor force, more work hasn’t translated into pay parity for Hispanic women. Despite upward progress in 2025’s data, Hispanic women still only earn just under 60 cents to every dollar earned by their non-Hispanic white male peers.


### **What it will take**


The 2025 narrowing of the gender wage gap and the surge in women’s nonfarm and healthcare employment mark significant progress. As the gap between women’s and men’s labor force participation has improved, and women’s nonfarm employment has risen across 2026, we could see the wage gap take another meaningful step towards parity in 2026. However, progress to full pay parity will require addressing persistent racial disparities. More employment across the board doesn’t equal higher-paying jobs. While expanded opportunities in healthcare and higher educational attainment continue to drive overall gains, systemic setbacks—such as job losses that disproportionately affect Black women and ongoing wage gaps for Hispanic and Black women—demonstrate that overall progress remains uneven. Real change means getting women—especially Black women and Hispanic women—into the higher-paying jobs, not just more jobs overall.


### **Methodology**


This report compiled data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The overall gender wage gap is calculated by comparing median earnings for all full-time, year-round working women to all full-time, year-round working men. Racial gender wage gaps are measured by comparing median earnings for full-time, year-round working women in specific racial and ethnic groups to non-Hispanic white men working full-time, year-round.
